content: Dyspepsia, derived from the Greek words dysmeaning difficult and pepsis meaning digestion, refers to chronic or recurrent pain or discomfort localized in the upper abdomen. Discomfort in this context encompasses mild pain, a sensation of upper abdominal fullness, and early satiety during meals. It may also be accompanied by symptoms such as bloating, belching, nausea, or heartburn. However, heartburn is excluded from the definition of dyspepsia in ICD-10, as it typically has a distinct etiology and management approach. Dyspepsia is a common condition, often influenced by lifestyle factors such as smoking and dietary habits. However, it can also result from serious underlying causes, including gastric cancer, peptic ulcer disease, or the use of certain medications. In cases where dyspepsia occurs without risk factors for serious conditions, it is termed undiagnosed dyspepsia and may be managed without extensive diagnostic investigations. If investigations fail to identify a specific cause, the condition is classified as functional dyspepsia. The understanding of dyspepsia's pathogenesis began with the first description of gastric ulcer disease in 1799. The term dyspepsia in its current form was introduced by Walter Alvarez in 1916. Dyspepsia is broadly categorized into two types: ulcer dyspepsia and non-ulcer dyspepsia, the latter also referred to as functional dyspepsia. The mechanisms underlying functional dyspepsia may involve heightened stress responsiveness due to early-life environmental factors, genetic predispositions, residual inflammation following gastrointestinal infections, or other causes. These processes are further influenced by factors such as psychophysiological abnormalities, abnormal gastric acid secretion, Helicobacter pylori infection, dietary habits, and lifestyle. Life-threatening causes of dyspepsia include coronary artery disease and ischemic bowel disease. Other common causes include gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), gastritis, lactose intolerance, and peptic ulcers. Dyspepsia must be differentiated from other conditions presenting with epigastric pain, such as gastritis, GERD, acute pancreatitis, primary biliary cirrhosis, cholelithiasis, gastric outlet obstruction, myocardial infarction, pleural empyema, and appendicitis. The incidence of Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection, a common cause of dyspepsia, varies geographically. In developing countries, the annual incidence ranges from 3,000 to 10,000 per 100,000 individuals. The prevalence of H. pylori infection increases with age. In the United States, approximately 20% of adolescents are infected, compared to 90% of children under five years of age in developing countries. H. pylori-associated gastritis is more prevalent among African Americans (54%), Hispanics (52%), and the elderly compared to Whites (21%). Acute gastritis tends to affect females more frequently, while H. pylori-associated gastritis is more common in males. High rates of H. pylori infection are observed in countries such as Japan, Colombia, Costa Rica, and China, while rates are comparatively lower in the United States. The infection is also prevalent in Southern and Eastern Europe, Mexico, South America, Africa, most Asian countries, and among Aboriginal populations in North America. Dyspepsia often persists throughout life, with spontaneous resolution being rare. It is most commonly associated with H. pylori infection. The prevalence of dyspepsia increases with age and varies among different ethnic groups. Persistent dyspepsia is linked to an increased risk of developing duodenal and peptic ulcers. Complications of dyspepsia include peptic ulcers, anemia due to gastritis, gastric cancer, vitamin B12 deficiency, and pernicious anemia. Functional dyspepsia, despite being a chronic condition, has an excellent prognosis regardless of H. pylori infection status. The clinical presentation of dyspepsia includes upper abdominal pain or burning, nausea, bloating, excessive belching, heartburn, fever, a metallic taste, stomach rumbling, early satiety, a sensation of food being stuck in the esophagus, pain or discomfort in the xiphoid region, and chills resembling those experienced during fevers. On physical examination, patients may appear pale, fatigued, or distressed, particularly if abdominal pain is present. Vital signs are typically normal, but tachycardia may occur in cases of gastrointestinal bleeding. Conjunctival pallor may be observed in patients with melena or hematemesis. Halitosis may be noted in chronic gastritis, and epigastric tenderness may be present. Gastritis associated with gastric ulcers may lead to blood loss, with stool tests potentially being guaiac-positive. There is no specific laboratory test for diagnosing dyspepsia. Laboratory investigations are primarily used to rule out bleeding, confirm the success of eradication therapy, or evaluate refractory ulcers. Imaging studies, such as esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), are typically reserved for patients over 55 years of age or those with alarm features. EGD involves examining the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum using an endoscope to exclude conditions such as peptic ulcer disease, medication-related ulceration, malignancy, and other rare causes. Treatment for functional and undifferentiated dyspepsia is similar. The use of drug therapy, particularly proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), is debated due to the inclusion of heartburn in some clinical trials, which may have skewed results. Surgical intervention is not recommended for managing dyspepsia. Primary prevention strategies for dyspepsia include avoiding long-term use of medications such as NSAIDs, abstaining from alcohol, quitting smoking, reducing consumption of coffee, acidic beverages, and spicy foods, and managing stress. Adopting healthy eating habits, regular exercise, and maintaining a healthy body weight may also help prevent dyspepsia. Secondary prevention strategies following H. pylori infection include the use of antibiotics to prevent recurrence of infection and post-treatment confirmation of H. pylori eradication using diagnostic tests. Routine screening for dyspepsia is not currently recommended due to insufficient evidence.
